meta.title: Overlap-add and overlap-save: fast long-signal filtering
meta.tools: Own overlap-add and overlap-save block convolvers (NumPy rfft), direct convolution reference, block-size sweep and operation-count model
meta.summary: Implement both block-convolution methods, verify they reproduce direct filtering exactly, and measure the speed-up over direct convolution as a function of block size — predicted from an operation-count model.
meta.problem: Filtering a million-sample signal with a 256-tap filter: direct, one giant FFT, or blocks? And what block size is best?
meta.theory:
Per output sample, direct convolution costs M multiply-adds. With FFT size L and M taps, each block yields L−M+1 new samples at the cost of one forward and one inverse FFT
(≈ 2·(L/2)·log₂L complex operations for real FFTs) plus L/2 products, so cost/sample ≈ $\frac{L(\log_2L+1)}{L-M+1}$ — minimised near L ≈ 4–8 M. For M = 256: predicted optimum L ≈ 2048,
speed-up vs direct ≈ M / min(cost) ≈ 256/13 ≈ 20× in operations.
meta.method: x: 2²⁰ Gaussian samples; h: 256-tap windowed-sinc low-pass. OLA and OLS with L = 512 … 65536; reference np.convolve. Wall time vs L; error vs reference.
